episodes.title: Meet Sena and Daniel: What AI Can't Do for You
Reading Emotions on a Video Call

brief_data.summary: Sena's ten-minute presentation to Mark's team went well ("This is exactly what we needed"), but in the Q&A she froze for seven seconds on one English sentence and said "two weeks" when Wendell's region three numbers need three, and Wendell corrected her in the chat. That night she replays the recording again and again, until Daniel asks what she would tell her friend Misaki after the same meeting. He shares Breines and Chen's experiments, where students who read three self-compassionate sentences after failing a test studied about 50% longer, and Grossmann and Kross's "Solomon's paradox," where people reasoned more wisely about a friend's problem than their own until they used their own name. Daniel tells how joking about his own mistake for months taught his team that mistakes follow you, and they compare Japan's "be strict with yourself, kind to others" with the American "give yourself some grace." Today's challenge: on a day something goes wrong, write yourself the same words you'd write to a friend.
brief_data.hook:
The presentation went well, but you froze for seven seconds in the Q&A, and now you're replaying it at night.
Learn to write yourself three kind, honest sentences after a mistake, the way you'd write to a friend.
brief_data.thumb_sub: Talk to Yourself Like a Friend

brief_data.short_title: Reading Emotions on a Video Call
brief_data.summary: On Friday morning in Tokyo, Sena joins her first weekly video sync with Mark's team, and when Mark jokes "Let's not let that become four!" about the region three timeline, Wendell goes still, answers "Yep" and "It's in the doc," and turns his camera off. Daniel shares Eyal, Steffel and Epley's 25 experiments, where imagining another person's perspective didn't make people more accurate but asking did, and Kraus's finding that people read emotions slightly better from the voice alone than from voice and face together. He tells the story of Nadia, who smiled on every call until she asked for a transfer, and they compare Japan's "reading the air" and silent canned coffee with the American habit of asking out loud. Today's challenge: notice one person whose energy changes in a meeting, then send them a short private message afterward.
brief_data.hook:
A coworker goes quiet and turns off their camera right after a joke in the meeting. Are they angry with you, or is it something else?
Learn how to notice a change in someone on a call, listen to their voice, and send one short message that asks instead of guessing.
